newsitem.title: USA: Board limits outdoor cigarette ads in Seattle area.
newsitem.headline: Board limits outdoor cigarette ads in Seattle area.

text.p: Cigarette advertising on billboards will be banned in much of Seattle under health regulations approved Friday which are aimed at reversing a recent increase in smoking by minors.

The King County Board of Health voted unanimously to ban tobacco advertising within 2,000 feet of schools, playgrounds and parks that have playgounds as the first step of a programme to restrict tobacco use and advertising.

The board originally had proposed banning tobacco billboards within 1,000 feet of schools and playgrounds but decided to double the distance to provide a "stronger level of protection," said panel Chairman Greg Nickels.

"The tobacco industry has targeted our kids as its next generation of customers," Nickels said. "Fundamentally, the Board of Health is saying, 'That's wrong,' and we will do everything within our power to prevent them from targeting our kids in this manner."
The move by King County, the state's biggest with nearly one-third of its residents, is one of the strongest actions taken by a municipality to restrict tobacco advertising.

In Pierce County, which includes Tacoma, the tobacco industry has challenged restrictions that limit outdoor advertising to black-and-white "tombstone" lettering. The city of Baltimore limits tobacco billboards to industrial and commercial zones.

Under the Board of Health's original proposal, 27 percent of Seattle billboards would have been off-limits for tobacco advertising. Officials had not yet recalculated the figure, but Nickels said it was "reasonable" to conclude that nearly the entire city would be covered.

Officials of AK Media/NW, which owns most of the billboards in Seattle and King County, argued that the industry's current voluntary 500-foot setback from schools and playgrounds was sufficient to protect children.

"We do not feel that additional government regulations are necessary," said Randy Swain, president of the company, a division of Ackerley Group Inc. He said an anti-smoking campaign aimed at children would be more effective way to prevent underage smoking.
Anti-smoking activists long have argued the tobacco industry targets minors, a claim conceded by Liggett Group in its settlement of litigation with 23 states and other plaintiffs.
This week, the Federal Trade Commission demanded that R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. extinguish "Joe Camel" cartoon ads, which it called an illegal effort to promote smoking among children.

The local moves on advertising ultimately could be pre-empted by settlement negotiations under way between the tobacco companies and 30 states. Officials have said any settlement likely would include a broad ban on tobacco advertising.
The King County billboard restrictions are scheduled to go into effect Aug. 15, although Nickels said a legal challenge is likely.

In July, the health board will consider regulations limiting in-store advertising and requiring cigarettes to be stored behind the counter. The board also plans to consider a ban on smoking in restaurants.
